privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: Variater is a tool for modelling leveraged buyouts. This page says what it keeps about you, who handles it for us, and how to have it removed.
privacy.storedSignIn: Sign-in is run by Clerk. Clerk holds your email address and, if you sign in with Google, the name and picture Google shares. Variater's own database keeps only Clerk's id for you, never your name or email address.
privacy.storedProfile: The four answers you give when you sign up: country, preferred currency, number format and time zone. And one choice: whether you want your usual figures suggested (Deal, Inputs, Starting point). The suggestions themselves are never kept: each time you open a deal they are worked out from your own saved deals in the same region and sector. Nobody else's deals are read for you, and yours are never read for anyone else. Switch it off and your deals are not read for it at all.
privacy.storedDeals: The deals you save, their earlier versions, the actual results you enter for them, and your settings. With each deal and version we keep which version of the model it was saved with and the IRR and MOIC it gave then, so reopening it can tell you if its results have changed. Nothing from a deal is ever written to a log or an error report.
privacy.storedActivity: A history of what you did and when: a deal created, edited (which fields, never the figures), renamed, archived, a version kept or restored, actual results saved, a download, a deal deleted, changes to your settings, letting a deal count in model validation or stopping it, switching suggestions of your usual figures on or off, and, for an administrator, showing or hiding the reference library and proposing, approving or rejecting a reference transaction (public filing data; the library keeps which account reviewed it). It holds no figures, deal names or version labels, so it outlives a deleted deal without keeping anything from it. A file uploaded or deleted is one line too, without the file's name.
privacy.storedFiles: The documents you upload (Deal, Documents): the file itself, in a private store only our server holds the key to, and beside it the name you gave it, its kind, its size and whether it passed its check. Nothing is read out of a file and kept, and no file name or link is ever written to a log. Each file is checked on our server before it can be downloaded; one that is refused is deleted at once.
privacy.storedCoverage: The companies you follow (Equity research, Coverage) under the names you give them, and the results you accept for them: the figures of each statement, the page each came from, and which figures you corrected or accepted as read. Nothing from a read is kept until you accept it. The figures stay when the filing itself is deleted (90 days after upload), until you remove them. Also the sector model you save for each company, with its versions, and its results note: what you type for it (your view, target, argument and date) and the linking sentences last written, never a figure (those are read from the model each time the note is drawn). Your firm's name and disclosures, typed once for your notes.
privacy.storedAddin: If you use the Excel add-in: a sign-in of its own for each time you sign the add-in in, kept only as a one-way fingerprint with the time it ends (a working day later), so the stored copy can't sign anyone in. It reaches your coverage and uploading a results PDF to read, nothing else (not your deals or your other documents), and ends when you sign the add-in out. The add-in keeps that sign-in, and the email address you signed in with, in Excel's own browser storage on your computer; the cells it writes are in your workbook, not on our server.
privacy.storedAiUsage: How much of the AI you used, a day at a time: how many results pages and document pages were read and note sentences written for you, how many requests that took, the tokens counted and what they cost (or would cost) at the AI provider's price list. Only counts and amounts, never anything from a file or from what the AI answered. Kept for 400 days, so a year of results seasons can be compared; each night the totals for everyone together are added up without naming anyone.
privacy.validation: Off unless you switch it on for a deal (Backtest, Plan and actuals). Then, each night, that deal's plan and actual results are run through the model on our server to see whether its outcome fell inside the ranges it predicted. Only counts and rates per region, sector, size and era are kept in the report everyone signed in can see: never the deal, its name, its figures or your account, and a group with fewer than five users' deals shows neither its figures nor how many it holds. Switch it off and the next report leaves the deal out; deleting the deal does the same.
privacy.google: Google shares your name, email address and profile picture with Clerk, only so that you can sign in. Variater asks for nothing else from your Google account and never reads your Google data.
privacy.companies: A company search, and loading a company's figures, sends what you typed (a name, ticker, LEI, ISIN or company number) from our server to the public registers searched: the US SEC (EDGAR), filings.xbrl.org, GLEIF, UK Companies House and Japan's EDINET. They see our server asking, never who you are. The figures are public filings, kept in a store every account shares, with nothing about who asked for them.
privacy.reader: When you ask Variater to read a results filing you uploaded (Equity research, Coverage), our server sends that file and pictures of its statement pages to Google's Gemini models, which read the figures. While the reader runs on Google's free tier, Google may use what it is sent to improve its products, so you are asked to confirm the file is a listed company's published results before anything is sent. What the models answer is kept for six hours so you can see it, then deleted; nothing from the file is written to a log. A file bigger than 13 MB is held in Google's file store for the read and deleted as soon as it is done. The same holds when you ask Variater to read a document for a deal (Deal, From a document): the file and pictures of the pages it cites go to Google's Gemini models, you confirm it is public first, and the answer is kept six hours; nothing from it enters a deal until you accept each value. When you ask the AI to write a results note's linking sentences, it is sent only what each figure means and which way it moved ("revenue, current year", "higher than last year"), never the company, a figure, your view or anything from a filing.
privacy.processors: Clerk (sign-in), Vercel (the website), Render (the model API), Neon (the database, in the United States), Supabase (encrypted nightly backups, and the documents you upload), Upstash (usage counters, keyed by a one-way hash of your id), Google (reading the results filings you ask it to read, and writing a note's linking sentences when you ask), Sentry (error reports, with deal contents removed) and Better Stack (uptime checks).
privacy.not: No advertising, no selling or sharing of your data, and no tracking cookies: the only cookies are the ones that keep you signed in.
privacy.keep: Your deals, their actual results and your settings stay until you delete them or ask us to delete your account. A deleted deal's activity stays in your account's history until you ask us to delete your account; edits older than a week are merged into one line a day. An uploaded document is deleted when you delete it, and otherwise 90 days after it was uploaded. Counts of AI use go after 400 days. Encrypted backups are rotated and the oldest is at most a year old.
privacy.contact: To have your account and everything in it deleted, or to ask anything about this policy, open an issue at <link></link>.

support.title: Support
support.intro: Help with Variater and its Excel add-in: how to ask a question or report a problem, what the add-in does, and what you need to use it.
support.help: To ask a question, report a problem or suggest a change, open an issue at <link></link>. We read every one and answer there.
support.helpPublic: Issues are public, so describe what you did and what you saw, but never paste figures from your deals, your files or anything you would not publish.
support.what: Variater is a modelling tool for investment professionals. Its equity research workspace reads a listed company's published results filing, lets you check every figure beside the page it came from, keeps the quarters you accept, and builds a sector model, a valuation and a results note from them. It drafts; the view, the target and the argument are always yours.

explain.returns_money: The sponsor puts <f>{equityIn}</f> of equity in at close and takes <f>{equityOut}</f> out at exit, <f>{hold}</f> years later (amounts in {money}). That is <f>{moic}</f> the money put in, an IRR of <f>{irr}</f> a year.
explain.returns_clears: Against the <f>{hurdle}</f> hurdle the IRR is <f>{diff}</f> points: it clears it.
explain.returns_misses: Against the <f>{hurdle}</f> hurdle the IRR is <f>{diff}</f> points: it falls short.
explain.returns_exit: At exit the business is valued at <f>{exitEv}</f>: <f>{ebitda}</f> of EBITDA at <f>{multiple}</f>. Net debt of <f>{netDebt}</f> is settled out of that value before the equity (a figure below zero is net cash, which adds to it).
explain.returns_bridge: The bridge splits the change from the equity put in to the equity taken out into its causes: fees, EBITDA growth, a change in the multiple and debt paid down.
explain.sensitivity_base: Each cell reruns the whole deal at one exit multiple and one hold. The outlined cell is this deal: <f>{multiple}</f> held <f>{hold}</f>, an IRR of <f>{irr}</f>.
explain.sensitivity_noBase: Each cell reruns the whole deal at one exit multiple and one hold. This deal's own exit multiple or hold is outside the grid, so no cell is outlined.
explain.sensitivity_range: Across the grid the IRR runs from <f>{low}</f> to <f>{high}</f>. Green cells clear the <f>{hurdle}</f> hurdle; red ones fall short of it.
explain.debt_raise: The deal borrows <f>{atClose}</f> at close, <f>{share}</f> of its enterprise value.
explain.debt_repay: By exit <f>{atExit}</f> is still owed, so <f>{repaid}</f> of the debt has been repaid. Repayments come out of levered free cash flow: <f>{cumFcf}</f> over <f>{years}</f> years.
explain.credit_first: In <f>{year}</f>, EBIT divided by interest is <f>{coverage}</f> and debt is <f>{leverage}</f> EBITDA. The weaker of the two sets the rating band: <f>{band}</f>.
explain.credit_last: By <f>{year}</f> the band is <f>{band}</f>. Repaying debt and growing EBITDA move it up; more debt or falling profit move it down.
explain.credit_shown: S&P's default studies put the chance of default by <f>{year}</f>, for a company in these bands, at <f>{cumulative}</f>.
explain.credit_hidden: The chances of default are not shown: on past deals in this region they did no better than a simpler measure, so the tile says so instead of guessing.
explain.mc_centre: The simulation runs the deal <f>{paths}</f> times, each with its own draw of growth, exit multiple, rates and margin. The mean IRR is <f>{mean}</f> and the median <f>{median}</f>.
explain.mc_tails: One path in twenty ends below <f>{p5}</f> and one in twenty above <f>{p95}</f>: the spread a plan built on the means alone does not show.
explain.mc_hurdle: <f>{above}</f> of the paths clear the <f>{hurdle}</f> hurdle.
explain.mc_wipeout: In <f>{wipeout}</f> of the paths the equity is lost altogether.
explain.drivers_strongest_up: {driver} moves the IRR most: a rank correlation of <f>{rho}</f>, so paths with more of it tend to end with a higher IRR.
explain.drivers_strongest_down: {driver} moves the IRR most: a rank correlation of <f>{rho}</f>, so paths with more of it tend to end with a lower IRR.
explain.drivers_meaning: A rank correlation runs from minus one to one. It says how often two things move together, not how much one causes the other.
explain.tail_downside: In the worst <f>{share}</f> of paths the IRR averages <f>{total}</f>, against <f>{base}</f> when every driver sits at its mean.
explain.tail_upside: In the best <f>{share}</f> of paths the IRR averages <f>{total}</f>, against <f>{base}</f> when every driver sits at its mean.
explain.tail_largest: {driver} accounts for the largest part of the gap: <f>{points}</f> points.
explain.tail_adds: The bars add up to the whole gap, so each is that driver's own share of it.
explain.value_dcf: Discounting the forecast cash flows at <f>{rate}</f> a year, with growth of <f>{growth}</f> a year after the last forecast year, gives <f>{dcf}</f> a share.
explain.value_multiple_pe: Earnings in <f>{year}</f> at <f>{multiple}</f> give <f>{mps}</f> a share.
explain.value_multiple_ev_ebitda: EBITDA in <f>{year}</f> at <f>{multiple}</f>, less net debt and non-controlling interests, gives <f>{mps}</f> a share.
explain.value_price: Set against the price typed, <f>{price}</f>, the first value is <f>{gapDcf}</f> away and the second <f>{gapMult}</f>.
explain.value_noPrice: No price is typed, so neither value is set against one.
explain.value_none: Both are the model's arithmetic on the assumptions typed; the tool forms no view of the shares.
explain.model_how: The cells you can type in are figures from the filings and the assumptions; every other cell is a formula, shown on hover, the same as in the workbook.

glossary.irr: Internal rate of return: the yearly return that makes the equity put in at close worth exactly what comes out at exit.
glossary.moic: Multiple of invested capital: the equity taken out at exit divided by the equity put in at close.
glossary.equityIn: The sponsor's cheque at close: the price and fees less the debt raised.
glossary.equityOut: What the sponsor takes out at exit: the exit value less net debt and exit costs.
glossary.exitEv: Enterprise value at exit: the business's value to all its lenders and owners, EBITDA at exit times the exit multiple.
glossary.netDebtAtExit: Debt still owed at exit less the cash the business holds; it is paid out of the exit value first.
glossary.equityBridge: How the equity put in becomes the equity taken out, step by step: fees, EBITDA growth, the change in the multiple and debt paid down.
glossary.irrSensitivity: The IRR the whole deal earns at each exit multiple and holding period, each cell a full rerun of the model.
glossary.exitMultiple: The multiple of EBITDA the business is sold for at exit.
glossary.debtPaydown: How much of each loan is still owed at close and at the end of each year.
glossary.operatingSummary: The business's main figures each year of the hold, as the model projects them.
glossary.revenue: Sales in the year: what the business is paid for its goods and services.
glossary.ebitda: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: operating profit with the non-cash charges added back.
glossary.ebitdaAfterLeases: EBITDA once rent on leases is paid. Under IFRS 16 reported EBITDA leaves lease costs out, so the model takes them off to compare like with like.
glossary.ebitdaMargin: EBITDA as a share of revenue.
glossary.interest: Interest paid on the deal's debt in the year, with any commitment fees.
glossary.financeCosts: The IFRS name for interest expense: the cost of the company's borrowing in the year.
glossary.leveredFcf: Levered free cash flow: cash the business makes after interest, tax, capex and working capital, before any debt is repaid.
glossary.leases: What the deal's leases do to its value: the lease cost, the EBITDA the multiple values and the liability counted as debt.
glossary.leaseCost: What the leases cost a year: rent, or under IFRS 16 the depreciation and interest on leased assets.
glossary.valuationEbitda: The EBITDA the multiple is applied to, before or after lease costs depending on the lease view chosen.
glossary.entryEv: Enterprise value at close: the price paid for the whole business, before deducting any debt.
glossary.leaseLiability: The present value of the lease payments still to make, carried on the balance sheet under IFRS 16.
glossary.netDebtAtEntry: Debt at close less cash, with the lease liability when leases count as debt.
glossary.debtAtClose: All the debt the deal raises at close, across every loan.
glossary.debtAtExit: The debt still owed at the end of the hold, before the exit repays it.
glossary.interestYear1: Interest paid in the first year of the hold, across every loan.
glossary.cumulativeFcf: Levered free cash flow added up over the hold so far.
glossary.interestLoop: Interest depends on debt, and debt on the cash left after interest; the model repeats the sum until the two agree to within a cent.
glossary.debtBalance: The deal's debt by loan, at close and at each year end.
glossary.cashFlow: From profit to the cash that can repay debt, year by year.
glossary.netIncome: Profit after interest and tax: what is left for the owners in the year.
glossary.profitForYear: The IFRS name for net income: profit after interest and tax for the year.
glossary.da: Depreciation and amortisation: the cost of assets spread over the years they are used. It costs no cash in the year, so it is added back.
glossary.capex: Capital expenditure: cash spent on equipment, buildings and other long-lived assets.
glossary.changeInNwc: Cash tied up in, or released from, working capital: receivables and inventory less payables.
glossary.capitalStructure: Each loan in the deal: its size, price, term and how it is repaid.
glossary.facility: A loan in the deal, with its own terms.
glossary.facilityAmount: How much the loan lends at close; for a revolver, how much is drawn of its commitment.
glossary.timesEbitda: The loan's size as a multiple of EBITDA at close.
glossary.facilityRate: The loan's interest rate in the first year: the reference rate, floored, plus the margin, or the fixed coupon.
glossary.maturity: How many years until the loan must be repaid in full.
glossary.sweepShare: The share of spare cash this loan takes each year to repay itself early.
glossary.pikShare: Payment in kind: the share of interest added to the loan instead of paid in cash.
glossary.opening: What is owed on the loan at the start of the year.
glossary.mandatory: Repayments the loan's terms require each year, whatever the cash.
glossary.cashSweep: Early repayment from spare cash, beyond what the terms require.
glossary.closing: What is owed on the loan at the end of the year.
glossary.cashInterest: The part of the interest paid in cash.
glossary.pikAccrued: Interest added to the loan instead of paid, so the loan grows.
glossary.commitmentFee: The fee a revolver charges on the part of its commitment not drawn.
glossary.redrawn: Cash drawn again on a revolver in the year to cover a shortfall.
glossary.close: The day the deal completes: the debt raised then, before any repayment.
glossary.distress: Each year's credit standing: how well profit covers interest, how high the debt is and the rating band they point to.
glossary.interestCover: EBIT divided by interest: how many times the year's operating profit pays the interest.
glossary.leverage: Debt at the start of the year divided by the year's EBITDA.
glossary.coverageBand: The rating band that interest cover alone points to, from Damodaran's table of coverage ratios.
glossary.leverageBand: The rating band that leverage alone points to, from S&P's corporate methodology and the business risk chosen.
glossary.ratingBand: The weaker of the coverage and leverage bands: the credit rating the year's figures look like.
glossary.defaultChance: The chance of default in that year for a company in the year's band, from S&P's default study.
glossary.defaultCumulative: The chance of default in that year or any year before it.
glossary.distressSimulated: Across the simulated paths: the share in each rating band each year.
glossary.pathsAt: The share of simulated paths whose figures that year read as this rating band.
glossary.meanDefaultChance: The chance of default in the year, averaged over every simulated path.
glossary.meanDefaultCumulative: The chance of default by the year, averaged over every simulated path.
glossary.meanIrr: The average IRR across every simulated path.
glossary.aboveHurdle: The share of simulated paths whose IRR is above the hurdle rate, the return the deal must earn.
glossary.p5: The fifth percentile: one path in twenty ends with a lower IRR.
glossary.p95: The ninety-fifth percentile: one path in twenty ends with a higher IRR.
glossary.wipeout: The share of paths in which the equity is lost altogether.
glossary.runTime: How long the simulation took on the server.
glossary.irrDistribution: How the simulated IRRs spread: each bar is the share of paths in that range of IRR.
glossary.irrByPercentile: The IRR at each percentile of the paths, from the worst to the best.
glossary.moicDistribution: How the simulated multiples of money spread; below one, the equity loses money.
glossary.whatSimulated: The assumptions each path draws from: a mean and a spread for each, and the rest of the deal as entered.
glossary.simGrowth: Revenue growth a year: each path draws its own around this mean.
glossary.simExit: The exit multiple: each path draws its own around this mean.
glossary.simRate: The interest rate: each path draws its own around this mean, which moves floating loans only.
glossary.simMargin: Gross margin: each path draws its own around this mean.
glossary.simDebt: Debt as a share of the price, and the senior share of that debt.
glossary.simFacilities: The loans the deal lists, and how many of them pay a floating rate.
glossary.simFees: Transaction fees as a share of the price, then financing fees as a share of the debt.
glossary.simCosts: Operating costs, depreciation, capex and working capital, each as a share of revenue.
glossary.simTax: The tax rate on profit before tax.
glossary.whatMovesIrr: Each driver's rank correlation with the IRR across the paths: how strongly the two rise and fall together.
glossary.irrAgainst: Every path's IRR against the driver's draw, with the straight line that fits them best.
glossary.correlations: How the drivers' draws moved together in the paths, from minus one to one.
glossary.tailDownside: The worst paths, and how much each driver did to put them there.
glossary.tailUpside: The best paths, and how much each driver did to put them there.
glossary.irrAtMean: The IRR of one run with every driver at its mean.
glossary.tailMeanIrr: The average IRR of the paths in this tail.
glossary.valueDcf: A share's value from the forecast cash flows discounted to last year's balance sheet, less net debt and non-controlling interests, divided by the shares.
glossary.valueMultiple: A share's value from the multiple the analyst typed applied to a forecast year's earnings or EBITDA.
glossary.priceTyped: The share price the analyst typed, with its date; nothing fetches it.
glossary.valuation: The two ways the model values a share, from the assumptions typed in last year's column.
glossary.sectorModel: The company's model: rows of figures from its filings, the analyst's assumptions and the formulas that project them.
glossary.modelRow: What the line holds, in the sector's own words.
glossary.modelUnit: The line's unit: money in the company's own unit, a count, days, a share or a multiple.
glossary.ifrs: International Financial Reporting Standards, used in most countries outside the United States.
glossary.usGaap: US generally accepted accounting principles, the standard for companies reporting in the United States.
glossary.indAs: Indian Accounting Standards: India's version of IFRS, used by listed and larger Indian companies.
glossary.unit_thousands: Amounts are in thousands of the currency: 1,000 of the currency is shown as 1.
glossary.unit_lakhs: Amounts are in lakhs, an Indian unit: one lakh is a hundred thousand (1,00,000) of the currency.
glossary.unit_millions: Amounts are in millions of the currency: 1,000,000 of the currency is shown as 1.
glossary.unit_crores: Amounts are in crores, an Indian unit: one crore is a hundred lakhs, or 10 million (1,00,00,000) of the currency.
glossary.unit_billions: Amounts are in billions of the currency: a thousand million of the currency is shown as 1.
glossary.kind_amortising_term_loan: A bank loan repaid in instalments over its life, usually senior and floating rate.
glossary.kind_institutional_term_loan: A term loan sold to funds, repaid mostly at maturity with a small yearly amortisation.
glossary.kind_unitranche: One loan in place of senior and junior debt, from a direct lender, at a blended margin.
glossary.kind_second_lien: A loan secured on the same assets as the senior debt but repaid after it, so priced higher.
glossary.kind_senior_notes: Bonds sold to investors at a fixed coupon, usually repaid in full at maturity.
glossary.kind_pik_notes: Notes whose interest is added to the principal instead of paid in cash.
glossary.kind_vendor_loan: Part of the price the seller leaves in the business as a loan.
glossary.kind_revolver: A revolving credit facility: a commitment the business can draw, repay and draw again, paying a fee on the undrawn part.
glossary.kind_shareholder_loan: A loan from the owners, repaid after every other lender.
glossary.tranche_SeniorTermLoan: The senior loan: repaid first, secured on the business, priced at the base rate plus a margin.
glossary.tranche_Mezzanine: Junior debt repaid after the senior loan, at a higher rate for the higher risk.
glossary.tranche_SeniorNotes: Bonds ranking with the senior debt, at a fixed coupon.
glossary.bridgeAxis_Entry: The equity put in at close.
glossary.bridgeAxis_Fees: Transaction and financing fees, which reduce the equity's value at once.
glossary.bridgeAxis_EBITDAGrowth: The value added by EBITDA growing over the hold, at the entry multiple.
glossary.bridgeAxis_Multiple: The value added or lost by selling at a different multiple from the one paid.
glossary.bridgeAxis_Deleverage: The value passed to the equity by repaying debt from cash flow.
glossary.bridgeAxis_Exit: The equity taken out at exit.
glossary.driver_IRR: Internal rate of return: the yearly return on the equity put in.
glossary.driver_MOIC: Multiple of invested capital: equity out divided by equity in.
glossary.driver_Growth: The path's revenue growth a year.
glossary.driver_ExitMultiple: The path's multiple of EBITDA at exit.
glossary.driver_Interest: The path's interest rate, which moves floating loans only.
glossary.driver_GrossMargin: The path's gross margin: revenue less the cost of what is sold, as a share of revenue.
glossary.driver_EBITDAShock: A one-year fall or rise in EBITDA that the path draws once.

reader.closedBody: The reader opens here once it has met its accuracy bar on filings nobody tuned it on: no wrong figure left unflagged and under 3% of figures amber.

reader.howBody: Upload a quarterly results PDF (Documents keeps it, after its scan). One AI model reads the whole filing and finds the statements; a second, different model reads pictures of those pages again. Every figure the two reads give differently, that fails a sum the statement states, that leaves the balance sheet or the cash flow out of step, that differs from a quarter you already accepted, or that sits on a poorly scanned page without a sum to confirm it, is amber. You then review it with the page beside the figures; nothing is kept until you accept the quarter.

models.valuationHow: As at the end of last year: net debt, non-controlling interests and the shares are last year's balance sheet, from the accepted results, and each year's cash flow from the current year on is discounted to it. Type the discount rate, the growth after the forecast, the target multiple and the price with its date in last year's column of the model below; each is a yellow cell in the workbook too.
models.valuationDcf: Value per share, discounted cash flow
models.valuationDcfSub: Discount rate {rate}, growth after the forecast {growth}
models.valuationNoValue: no value until its assumptions are typed
models.valuationTypePrice: Type the price and its date in the model below
models.valuationNoDate: Type the price's date in the model below

models.riskFreeUse: Start the discount rate from it
models.riskFree_no_currency: No risk-free rate to offer: the accepted results are in no single currency yet.
models.riskFree_no_country: No risk-free rate to offer: the results' currency is not one country's we hold figures for.
models.riskFree_no_data: No risk-free rate to offer: no 10-year yield is stored for the results' country.
models.riskFreeCovered: A company kept in coverage is offered its country's 10-year government yield as a starting point.

report.limit: The sentences were written as often as allowed today. Try again tomorrow; the templates write them meanwhile.
report.refused_no_model: This company has no saved model yet. Build one on Coverage → Model; the note is drawn from it.
report.refused_no_version: That version of the model doesn't exist. Pick another one to compare with.
report.refused_not_found: This company isn't in your coverage.

report.refused_label_differs: A name in the note didn't match the model's, so the note was not drawn. Reload the page and try again.
report.refused_typed_differs: A field you typed didn't come through as typed. Save it again.
report.refused_call_in_text: A sentence held words of a view the tool may not state, so the note was not drawn. Write the sentences again.
report.refused_no_model_values: The model has no revenue to draw a note from.
report.refused_failed: The note couldn't be drawn. Try again in a moment.
report.emptyBody: Pick a covered company with a saved model to see its note.
report.previewLabel: The note as it will be written
report.viewHint: Yours alone: typed here, written into the note as typed, and left empty until you type them.
report.targetInvalid: Type a number of zero or more.
report.sentencesHint: Short sentences joining the tables. The AI is sent only what each figure means and which way it moved, never the company or a figure; the app puts the figures in. A sentence that holds a number or a view is written by its template instead.

report.detailsHint: Typed once for every note you draft: your firm's name and the disclosures your regulator requires. Check the wording with your compliance adviser.
report.detailsFailed: Not saved. Check the firm name is at most 200 characters and try again.

documents.unmeasuredBody: Its accuracy is not yet proven here ({cases} evaluation documents so far). Check every value.
documents.howBody: Upload an annual report, a set of financial statements or an information pack (PDF, any language). Two AI models read it: the first the whole document, the second pictures of the pages the first cites. Every value comes with its page and the document's own words; it is amber when the reads differ, when its quote is not on its page, when its quote does not hold it or when the page is a poor scan. Nothing enters the deal until you accept it.

tips.acceptValue: Tick a value to take it into the deal. Nothing from the document enters the deal unless you tick it; amber ones need a closer look.
tips.accountCountry: Your country. A new deal starts there, and its tax, growth and interest rates are offered first.
tips.accountCurrency: The currency a new deal starts in. Any deal can be in any currency.
tips.accountGrouping: How long numbers are grouped: the locale's own way, in thousands, or in lakhs and crores.
tips.accountLocale: How numbers and dates are written, as a language tag such as en-GB or de-DE. It also sets the language of the screens where one is available.
tips.accountTimeZone: Your time zone, for the times shown beside saved versions and in the activity list.
tips.activityWholeAccount: Show the activity of every deal and of Settings, not just the deal that is open.
tips.actualExitSold: On once the company has been sold: the exit's value, net debt and equity are then compared with the plan.
tips.actualExit_exit_ev: The enterprise value the company was sold at.
tips.actualExit_irr: The return a year on the equity. Left empty, it is worked out from the figures above.
tips.actualExit_moic: Money back as a multiple of the money in. Left empty, it is worked out from the figures above.
tips.actualExit_net_debt_at_exit: Net debt at the sale: debt less cash, repaid out of the price.
tips.actualExit_sponsor_equity_entry: The equity the sponsor put in at close. Left empty, the plan's cheque is used.
tips.actualYears: How many years of actual results to compare with the plan, up to the plan's hold.
tips.actual_ebitda: Actual EBITDA for this year. Leave it empty when it is not known.
tips.actual_fcf: Actual free cash flow for this year, after interest and tax and before any debt is repaid.
tips.actual_net_income: Actual net income for this year. Leave it empty when it is not known.
tips.actual_revenue: The company's actual revenue for this year, in the plan's money. Leave a figure empty when it is not known.
tips.actual_total_debt: Total debt at the end of this year. Leave it empty when it is not known.
tips.actualsCsv: Upload actual results as a CSV in the same layout as the download: one row per year, one column per figure.
tips.addTrancheKind: The kind of facility to add. Each kind starts from its market's usual terms, which you can then change.
tips.autoUpdate: On, the model runs again a moment after every edit. Off, edits wait in a bar above the results until you run them.
tips.commandSearch: Type part of a screen's or a help article's name and press Enter to open the first match. Arrow keys move through the list.
tips.companySearch: A company's name, ticker, ISIN, LEI or register number. Every public register that covers it is searched.
tips.confirmPublic: Tick to confirm the document is public. Until billing is on, reading uses an AI service whose free tier may learn from what it reads.
tips.correctFigure: The figure as the page prints it, if the read got it wrong. It replaces the read when you accept.
tips.correlation: How strongly two drivers move together in the simulation, from -1 to 1. The matrix must stay valid, so extreme values may be pulled in.
tips.coverageNewCompany: The name of a company to start covering. Its accepted results and model are kept under it.
tips.currency: The currency every amount is in. Changing it relabels the money; it never converts amounts between currencies.
tips.dealName: The name the deal is saved under. Only you can see it, and you can rename it at any time.
tips.devUser: Any name of letters, numbers, dots and hyphens. Local runs only: each name is its own account.
tips.documentFile: One of your checked PDFs: an annual report, financial statements or an information pack, in any language.
tips.field_accounting_standard: The standard the EBITDA follows. Under IFRS 16 it is before lease costs, under US GAAP after them, which changes how leases are valued.
tips.field_ap_days: Payable days: how long the company takes to pay its suppliers, as days of cost of sales. Used when working capital comes from days.
tips.field_ar_days: Receivable days: how long customers take to pay, as days of revenue. Used when working capital comes from days.
tips.field_base_rate: The interest rate on the senior debt, a year. Mezzanine pays this plus the mezzanine spread.
tips.field_business_risk: S&P's business risk profile, from 1 (excellent) to 6 (vulnerable): how steady the business is. It sets how much leverage each rating band allows.
tips.field_capex: Capital expenditure as a percentage of revenue: cash spent on equipment and other long-lived assets each year.
tips.field_da: Depreciation and amortisation as a percentage of revenue. It lowers taxable profit but is not cash, so it is added back to cash flow.
tips.field_debt_pct: Debt raised at close as a percentage of the enterprise value; the sponsor's equity pays the rest. More debt raises the return and the risk.
tips.field_ebitda: The company's EBITDA for the last full year before the deal, in the deal's money. Every multiple, the debt and the forecast start from it.
tips.field_entry_mult: What the buyer pays, as a multiple of EBITDA: the enterprise value is EBITDA times this. A higher price means a bigger equity cheque and a lower return.
tips.field_exit_mult: The multiple of exit-year EBITDA the company is sold at. Setting it at or below the entry multiple keeps the return from relying on the market paying more later.
tips.field_gross_margin: Gross profit as a percentage of revenue: what is left after the cost of the goods or services sold.
tips.field_growth: Revenue growth a year over the hold, as a percentage. Sourced figures start it at the country's nominal GDP growth.
tips.field_hold: How many years the sponsor owns the company before selling it, from 1 to 15. The model projects each year and sells at the end of the last one.
tips.field_inv_days: Inventory days: how long stock sits before it is sold, as days of cost of sales. Used when working capital comes from days.
tips.field_lease_cost: What the company pays for its leases each year, in the deal's money. Held flat over the hold.
tips.field_lease_liability: The lease liability on the balance sheet at close, in the deal's money. On the post-IFRS 16 view it counts with net debt.
tips.field_lease_view: Pre-IFRS 16 values EBITDA after lease costs and leaves leases out of debt; post-IFRS 16 values it before them and counts the liability as debt.
tips.field_mezz_spread: What mezzanine pays above the senior rate, in percentage points, for being repaid after the senior debt.
tips.field_mincash: Cash the company must always keep, in the deal's money. The sponsor funds it at close and it is never used to repay debt.
tips.field_nwc: The increase in net working capital each year as a percentage of revenue: cash tied up in receivables and stock as the company grows.
tips.field_opex: Operating costs other than cost of sales and D&A, as a percentage of revenue. Gross margin less opex is the EBITDA margin.
tips.field_senior_pct: The share of the debt that is senior: repaid first and cheapest. The rest is mezzanine, priced at the senior rate plus its spread.
tips.field_tax: The tax rate on profit before tax. Tax rules below can cap interest deductions, carry losses forward or set a minimum tax.
tips.field_tax_interest_limit: Whether interest deductions are capped: none, a share of EBITDA (with an allowance), or a fixed amount a year.
tips.field_tax_interest_limit_amount: The allowance below which interest is always deductible, or with a fixed cap the most deductible a year, in the deal's money.
tips.field_tax_interest_limit_pct: With the EBITDA-share limit, the most net interest deductible in a year as a percentage of EBITDA; what is left over is carried forward.
tips.field_tax_loss_carryforward: On, a loss in one year reduces taxable profit in later years, within the limits below. Off, losses are simply lost.
tips.field_tax_loss_limit_amount: The profit a year that losses carried forward may always reduce in full, in the deal's money; above it the percentage limit applies.
tips.field_tax_loss_limit_pct: Above the allowance, the share of a year's profit that losses carried forward may reduce. 100% lets them reduce all of it.
tips.field_tax_minimum_pct: A minimum tax as a percentage of book profit: tax is raised to it in any year the rules would charge less. Zero means none.
tips.field_tax_preset: Fills the tax rate and rules with a country's headline rules as of their date. A starting point, not advice: check with a tax adviser.
tips.firstFiscalYear: The fiscal year of the first projected year, to label columns FY2026 and so on. Leave it empty to label them Y1, Y2.
tips.fiscalYearEnd: The month the fiscal year ends. Years are named by the year they end in: FY2025 for December, FY2024/25 otherwise.
tips.forecastStandard: The accounting standard the company reports under. It sets the statement words (finance costs, profit for the year) and travels with the company to a deal.
tips.forecast_ap_d: Payable days for each forecast year: how long the company takes to pay suppliers.
tips.forecast_ar_d: Receivable days for each forecast year: how long customers take to pay.
tips.forecast_buybacks: Shares to buy back in each forecast year, in the company's money.
tips.forecast_capex: Capital expenditure for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_da: Depreciation and amortisation for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_def_pct: Deferred revenue for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_divs: Dividends to pay in each forecast year, in the company's money.
tips.forecast_gm: Gross margin for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_h_ap: Trade payables at each historical year end: what the company still owes its suppliers.
tips.forecast_h_ar: Trade receivables at each historical year end: what customers still owe.
tips.forecast_h_buybacks: Shares bought back in each historical year.
tips.forecast_h_capex: Capital expenditure in each historical year, as the cash flow statement shows it.
tips.forecast_h_cash: Cash and equivalents at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_cogs: Cost of sales for each historical year, typed as a negative number.
tips.forecast_h_cs: Common stock and paid-in capital at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_da: Depreciation and amortisation for each historical year, as the cash flow statement adds it back.
tips.forecast_h_def: Deferred revenue at each historical year end: cash received for work not yet done.
tips.forecast_h_divs: Dividends paid in each historical year.
tips.forecast_h_int_exp: Interest the company paid on its debt in each historical year, typed as a negative number.
tips.forecast_h_int_inc: Interest the company earned on its cash in each historical year.
tips.forecast_h_inv: Inventory at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_lta: Goodwill and other long-term assets at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_ltd: Long-term debt at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_nca: Other non-current assets at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_ncl: Other non-current liabilities at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_oci: Accumulated other comprehensive income at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_ocl: Other current liabilities at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_ocurr: Other current assets at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_other: Other income or costs outside operations in each historical year (a cost negative).
tips.forecast_h_ppe: Property, plant and equipment, net of depreciation, at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_rd: Research and development costs for each historical year, typed as a negative number.
tips.forecast_h_re: Retained earnings at each historical year end.
tips.forecast_h_rev: Revenue for each historical year, as the company filed it. The forecast grows from the latest year.
tips.forecast_h_sbc: Stock-based compensation for each historical year, as the cash flow statement adds it back.
tips.forecast_h_sga: Selling, general and administrative costs for each historical year, typed as a negative number.
tips.forecast_h_tax: Income tax for each historical year, typed as a negative number.
tips.forecast_inv_d: Inventory days for each forecast year: how long stock sits before it is sold.
tips.forecast_ltd_chg: Debt raised (positive) or repaid (negative) in each forecast year, in the company's money.
tips.forecast_min_cash: The least cash the company keeps in each forecast year; below it, the revolver draws.
tips.forecast_nca_pct: Other non-current assets for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_ocl_pct: Other current liabilities for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_other_inc: Other income for each forecast year, in the company's money.
tips.forecast_r_cash: The interest rate earned on cash in each forecast year.
tips.forecast_r_debt: The interest rate paid on debt in each forecast year.
tips.forecast_rd: Research and development for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_rev_g: Revenue growth for each forecast year, as a percentage.
tips.forecast_sbc: Stock-based compensation for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_sga: Selling, general and administrative costs for each forecast year, as a percentage of revenue.
tips.forecast_tax: The tax rate on profit before tax for each forecast year.
tips.guidedName: The name the deal is saved under. You can rename it later on Deal, Saved deals.
tips.guidedSize: The company's EBITDA for its last full year, in the unit chosen beside it. It sets the deal's size; every other figure is a percentage or a multiple.
tips.latestFiscalYear: The fiscal year of the latest historical column, so the history and forecast are labelled by year. Leave it empty for LTM.
tips.librarySwitch: On, the reference library is shown to everyone; off, only administrators see it. Nothing in the deal model reads it.
tips.live_debt_pct: Move the debt as a share of the enterprise value. A listed structure is scaled to it, every facility alike.
tips.live_exit_mean: Move the average exit multiple the simulation draws around.
tips.live_exit_std: Move how widely the exit multiple is spread around its average: wider means more extreme outcomes.
tips.live_gross_margin_mean: Move the average gross margin the simulation draws around.
tips.live_growth_mean: Move the average revenue growth the simulation draws around. The estimate reruns the simulation of this deal.
tips.live_interest_mean: Move the average interest rate. On a listed structure, floating references move by the same distance.
tips.mcFixedSeed: On, the simulation draws the same random paths every run, so results repeat exactly. Off, each run draws new paths.
tips.mcSeed: The number that fixes the random draws. Any whole number; the same one always gives the same paths.
tips.mc_exit_mean: The average exit multiple the simulation draws around.
tips.mc_exit_std: How widely the exit multiple is spread around its average: about two thirds of paths fall within one of these.
tips.mc_gm_mean: The average gross margin the simulation draws around.
tips.mc_gm_std: How widely the gross margin is spread around its average, in percentage points.
tips.mc_growth_mean: The average revenue growth a year the simulation draws around.
tips.mc_growth_std: How widely revenue growth is spread around its average, in percentage points: about two thirds of paths fall within one of these.
tips.mc_hurdle: The return the sponsor needs, as a percentage IRR. The results show the share of paths that clear it.
tips.mc_n: How many random paths the simulation runs. More paths give steadier percentiles but take longer; 100,000 is the most.
tips.mc_rate_mean: The average interest rate the simulation draws around. Only floating facilities move with it.
tips.mc_rate_std: How widely the interest rate is spread around its average, in percentage points.
tips.mezzDebtMultiple: Mezzanine debt as a multiple of EBITDA. Changing it sets the debt and senior shares the model reads.
tips.modelAddLine: The way a new revenue line is worked out. Up to eight lines.
tips.modelAssumptionCell: An assumption that is yours to set (yellow). Every forecast formula reads it.
tips.modelChoice: A choice the company's filings settle, such as how a line is worked out backwards for the past. The model refuses an option that doesn't fit.
tips.modelCompanyName: The company's name, as the model and its workbook show it.
tips.modelComparison: Which roll forward to compare: the estimate made then beside the results that arrived.
tips.modelConstant: A fixed number the model needs, such as how many rupees a unit holds.
tips.modelCoveredCompany: Fill the past columns from a covered company's accepted results; choose none to type every figure.
tips.modelCurrency: The currency the company reports in, as a three-letter code such as INR.
tips.modelFigureCell: A figure typed from the company's documents. Change it to correct it; the formulas below rework at once.
tips.modelLine: How this revenue line is worked out: by occupancy, per tonne, per store and so on. Changing it keeps every other line.
tips.modelLineOff: Switch a revenue line off for this company when it has no such business; its rows stay in the model as zero.
tips.modelPlaces: Which line's places (beds, rooms, stores) or units sold the per-place and per-unit costs follow.
tips.modelScope: Use the consolidated figures (the group) or the standalone ones (the parent company alone).
tips.modelSector: The company's sector. It chooses which of the sector models is used and the words its rows are named with.
tips.modelStartFrom: Start a model for one of your covered companies, or open one of the examples solved by hand.
tips.modelUnit: The unit the company's figures are typed in, such as crores or millions.
tips.modelUnitName: How the statements name their money unit, as printed (for example 'Rs lakh').
tips.modelVersionLabel: An optional name for the version you keep now, such as 'Before the Q2 results'.
tips.moneyUnit: Whether amounts are typed in thousands, lakhs, millions, crores or billions. Changing it converts the amounts so the size stays the same.
tips.paneCompany: The covered company whose accepted results go into the sheet.
tips.panePeriod: The accepted period whose figures are written into the sheet, with their page numbers.
tips.proposeFile: A JSON file in the reference library's format. It joins the queue and needs two administrators' approval.
tips.readCompany: The covered company these results belong to; the accepted figures are kept under it.
tips.readFile: One of your checked PDFs: the company's results filing for a quarter or a year.
tips.readNewCompany: The name of a company to start covering. Only you can see your covered companies.
tips.readQuarter: The last day of the period the filing reports, such as the quarter's end.
tips.rejectReason: Why the proposal is refused. One rejection decides it, and the reason is kept with the review.
tips.reportArgument: Your argument for the rating, in your own words. It is printed as you write it.
tips.reportCompany: The covered company whose saved model the note is drafted from.
tips.reportCompare: The saved version whose estimates the note's changes are measured against.
tips.reportDate: The date printed on the note.
tips.reportDisclosures: The disclosures your firm prints on its research, typed once for the account and printed on every note.
tips.reportFirm: Your firm's name, printed on every note from this account.
tips.reportRating: Your rating, in your own words. The tool never suggests one; the note shows it exactly as typed.
tips.reportTarget: Your target value per share. The tool never works one out; it shows the number you type.
tips.seniorDebtMultiple: Senior debt as a multiple of EBITDA. Changing it sets the debt and senior shares the model reads.
tips.settings_bull_exit_mult: In the bull scenario, the exit multiple's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_bull_growth_mult: In the bull scenario, growth's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_bull_margin_mult: In the bull scenario, the gross margin's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_bull_rate_mult: In the bull scenario, the interest rate's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_def_base_rate: The senior interest rate a new deal starts with, before a benchmark rate is used.
tips.settings_def_capex: The capex share of revenue a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_da: The D&A share of revenue a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_debt_pct: The debt share of enterprise value a new deal starts with.
tips.settings_def_ebitda: The EBITDA a new deal starts with. Sourced figures or a document replace it; size is always yours to set.
tips.settings_def_entry_mult: The entry multiple a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_exit_mult: The exit multiple a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_gross_margin: The gross margin a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_growth: The revenue growth a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_hold: The hold, in years, a new deal starts with.
tips.settings_def_mezz_spread: The mezzanine spread over the senior rate a new deal starts with.
tips.settings_def_mincash: The minimum cash a new deal starts with, in the deal's money.
tips.settings_def_nwc: The working capital change a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_opex: The opex share of revenue a new deal starts with, before any sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_def_senior_amort: The share of the senior loan's original amount repaid each year before the cash sweep.
tips.settings_def_senior_pct: The senior share of the debt a new deal starts with.
tips.settings_def_tax: The tax rate a new deal starts with, before a country's rate is used.
tips.settings_fin_fee_pct: Fees for arranging the debt as a percentage of the debt raised, paid at close.
tips.settings_mc_clip_irr: On, extreme path IRRs are held between -100% and 500%, so a few wild paths don't distort the averages.
tips.settings_mc_exit_mean: The average exit multiple the simulation draws around.
tips.settings_mc_exit_std: How widely the exit multiple is spread in the simulation.
tips.settings_mc_gm_mean: The average gross margin the simulation draws around.
tips.settings_mc_gm_std: How widely the gross margin is spread in the simulation, in percentage points.
tips.settings_mc_growth_mean: The average revenue growth the simulation draws around, until a deal's sourced figures are used.
tips.settings_mc_growth_std: How widely growth is spread in the simulation, in percentage points.
tips.settings_mc_hurdle: The return a deal must clear, as an IRR. Results compare every deal and path with it.
tips.settings_mc_n: How many paths a Monte Carlo run uses by default. More paths give steadier results and take longer.
tips.settings_mc_n_passes: How many times each path reworks interest against the debt it pays down, from 1 to 10. More passes are closer and slower.
tips.settings_mc_rate_mean: The average interest rate the simulation draws around; only floating facilities move with it.
tips.settings_mc_rate_std: How widely the interest rate is spread in the simulation, in percentage points.
tips.settings_other_uses: Any other cash needed at close, in the deal's money: paid by the sponsor's equity like the fees.
tips.settings_rec_exit_mult: In the recession scenario, the exit multiple's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_rec_growth_adj: In the recession scenario, percentage points added to growth's average (usually a negative number).
tips.settings_rec_growth_floor: In the recession scenario, the lowest growth average the adjustment may reach.
tips.settings_rec_margin_mult: In the recession scenario, the gross margin's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_rec_rate_mult: In the recession scenario, the interest rate's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_sens_em_max: The highest exit multiple in the IRR sensitivity grid on Deal, Returns.
tips.settings_sens_em_min: The lowest exit multiple in the IRR sensitivity grid on Deal, Returns.
tips.settings_sens_em_steps: How many exit multiples the sensitivity grid shows between the lowest and the highest.
tips.settings_sens_hp_max: The longest hold in the sensitivity grid; each hold is a full run of the deal model.
tips.settings_sens_hp_min: The shortest hold in the sensitivity grid; each hold is a full run of the deal model.
tips.settings_stag_exit_mult: In the stagflation scenario, the exit multiple's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_stag_growth_adj: In the stagflation scenario, percentage points added to growth's average (usually a negative number).
tips.settings_stag_growth_floor: In the stagflation scenario, the lowest growth average the adjustment may reach.
tips.settings_stag_margin_mult: In the stagflation scenario, the gross margin's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_stag_rate_mult: In the stagflation scenario, the interest rate's average is multiplied by this.
tips.settings_tx_fee_pct: Advisory and other deal costs as a percentage of enterprise value, paid at close by the sponsor's equity.
tips.showArchived: Show archived deals in the list as well. Archiving hides a deal without deleting it, and it can be unarchived.
tips.startCountry: The company's country. It chooses the region whose industry figures, growth, tax rate and interest rates the sourced figures come from.
tips.startIndustry: The company's industry, from Damodaran's tables of listed companies. Its averages set the margins, multiples, capex and working capital.
tips.stockBasedComp: Stock-based compensation as a percentage of revenue, added back to show an adjusted EBITDA beside the model's. It changes no result.
tips.tranche_allow_redraw: On, a revolver may be drawn again to fund a year the cash falls short, within its commitment.
tips.tranche_amort_pct: The share of the original amount repaid each year before the sweep.
tips.tranche_amount: The facility's size, in the deal's money. For a revolver it is the commitment, of which only the drawn part is borrowed.
tips.tranche_commitment_fee_pct: For a revolver, a fee a year on the undrawn part of the commitment.
tips.tranche_drawn_pct: For a revolver, the share of the commitment drawn at close. Only the drawn part funds the deal; the undrawn part pays the commitment fee.
tips.tranche_fixed_rate: The interest rate a year on a fixed-rate facility.
tips.tranche_floating: On, the rate is a reference rate plus the margin, year by year; off, it is the fixed rate.
tips.tranche_floor: The lowest the reference rate may count as. The floor applies before the margin is added.
tips.tranche_kind: The kind of facility. Changing it applies that kind's usual terms; the list order is the order the cash sweep repays them in.
tips.tranche_margin: What the facility pays above its reference rate, in percentage points.
tips.tranche_maturity_years: Years until the facility must be repaid in full. It does not stretch with the hold.
tips.tranche_name: The facility's name, as schedules and downloads show it.
tips.tranche_pik_share: The share of the coupon paid in kind: added to the principal instead of paid in cash. It is still an expense.
tips.tranche_reference: The reference rate assumed for every year, as a percentage. Today's level is offered; a path by year can override it.
tips.tranche_reference_rate: The benchmark a floating facility is priced on: SOFR, SONIA, EURIBOR and so on. Choosing one starts it at today's level.
tips.tranche_reference_year: The reference rate assumed for this year. A path shorter than the hold repeats its last year.
tips.tranche_sweep: On, spare cash repays this facility early, in list order. Off, it is repaid only on its schedule.
tips.tranche_sweep_share: The most of the spare cash this facility takes each year; what it leaves goes to the next one.
tips.tranche_upfront_fee_pct: A fee paid at close as a percentage of the facility, on top of the deal's financing fees.
tips.uploadFiles: Choose PDF, Excel or Word files up to 20 MB each. Each is checked before it can be opened, and kept for 90 days.
tips.uploadPdf: Upload a PDF from this computer. It is checked before it is read, and kept with your documents.
tips.usualSwitch: On, the medians of your own saved deals in the same region and sector show beside the sourced figures. Nothing is learned or stored.
tips.validationConsent: On, this deal's plan and actual outcome may count, without anything that identifies it, in the model's accuracy report.
tips.versionLabel: An optional name for this version, such as 'Sent to committee', so it is easy to find and restore later.
tips.wspMode: On, working capital is worked out from receivable, inventory and payable days; off, from the NWC change percentage.

onboarding.guideIntro: Four questions, then the deal starts from published figures for the answers: industry margins and multiples for the region, the country's growth and tax rate, and the currency's interest rate. Every figure can be changed afterwards.
onboarding.why_region: The country chooses the region whose industry averages, growth, tax rate and interest rates the figures come from.
onboarding.why_sector: The industry's listed companies set the margins, the entry and exit multiples, capex and working capital. Choose the whole market if none fits.
onboarding.why_size: Its EBITDA for the last full year. Nothing free splits industry figures by size, so size sets the amounts but changes no percentage.
onboarding.question_currency: Which currency are its figures in?
onboarding.why_currency: The country's own currency is offered. The deal's amounts are in this currency; nothing is converted.
onboarding.question_figures: These are the figures the deal will start from
onboarding.why_figures: Each comes from the source named beside it. Name the deal and create it: it is saved to your account and opens on Deal, Inputs.
onboarding.sizeInvalid: Type the EBITDA as a number above zero.
onboarding.figuresFailed: The published figures could not be read just now. Try again in a minute; nothing has been saved.
onboarding.figuresTitle: Sourced figures for the guided deal
onboarding.figuresSummary: EBITDA {ebitda} {unit} of {currency}, and {count, plural, one {one figure} other {# figures}} from published data:
onboarding.missingFigure: No free source: the deal keeps its usual starting value.
onboarding.createFailed: The deal could not be saved. Try again.
onboarding.samplesIntro: The same four answers given in advance, in several regions and currencies. Each opens as a saved deal of yours with sourced figures; only its size is made up.
onboarding.figuresNote: Published figures describe listed companies in the region, not this company: treat them as a starting point and replace any you know better.
onboarding.sample_us_softwareNote: High margins and multiples; little capex.
onboarding.sample_de_machineryNote: An industrial in euros: long inventory days, modest growth.
onboarding.sample_gb_servicesNote: People-heavy and light on assets, in pounds.
onboarding.sample_in_hospitalsNote: Amounts in crores of rupees; faster nominal growth.
onboarding.sample_jp_electronicsNote: Amounts in billions of yen; low interest rates.
onboarding.sample_br_foodNote: High local interest rates make the debt expensive.

guides.savedStep1: Build a guided first deal: four answers, and it starts from published figures and saves itself.
guides.savedStep2: Or open a sample deal from another region to see how a finished deal reads.
guides.savedStep3: Or edit the deal on Deal, Inputs and save it here under a name; from then on every edit saves by itself.
guides.documentsStep1: Upload an annual report, financial statements or an information pack: PDF, Excel or Word, up to 20 MB each.
guides.documentsStep2: Each file is checked before it can be opened or read; anything that could run code is refused.
guides.documentsStep3: A checked PDF can be read for a deal on Deal, From a document, which shows every value with its page before anything enters the deal.
guides.documentsRead: Read a document for a deal
guides.coverageStep1: Add a company you cover, here.
guides.coverageStep2: Upload its results PDF on Results: it is read twice and every figure is shown beside its page for you to accept.
guides.coverageStep3: Build its sector model on Model, with the past filled from the quarters you accepted.
guides.coverageStep4: Draft a results note from the saved model on Report.

help.title: Help
help.intro: Each article is a section of the methodology: what the models do, in the order the code does it, with worked figures from the default deal. The articles are written in English and change whenever the methodology does.
help.whatsNewSummary: What has changed in the app, newest first.
help.whatsNewIntro: What has changed in the app that you would notice, newest first. Changes to how a number is calculated are also listed in the model's version history.
help.unseen: Something new since you last looked
help.summary_conventions: Years, timing, signs and rounding: the rules every calculation follows.
help.summary_inputs-units-and-settings: How money units and currencies are handled, what each input means and how Settings apply.
help.summary_the-deal-model: The deal model step by step: entry, the operating model, cash flow, the debt schedule, returns and the exit grid.
help.summary_the-deal-around-the-engine: What happens to your inputs before and after the engine runs: units, percentages, sources and uses.
help.summary_debt-structures-and-interest-rat: The nine kinds of facility, floating rates and floors, PIK, revolvers and the cash sweep.
help.summary_accounting-standards-and-leases: IFRS and US GAAP, and how leases change EBITDA, the valuation and net debt.
help.summary_tax-rules: Interest limits, losses carried forward, minimum taxes and the country presets.
help.summary_risk-warnings: The four warnings on Deal, Inputs and the published tables each one reads.
help.summary_monte-carlo-simulation: How the simulation draws growth, multiples, rates and margins, and where its ranges come from.
help.summary_plan-vs-actual: How a saved deal's plan is compared with what happened, and how the gap is split.
help.summary_three-statement-forecast: How the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow are projected and kept in balance.
help.summary_model-version: The stamp on every result, and why a saved deal can show different results today.
help.summary_estimates-the-ml-panels-and-fili: The risk score, distress, multiple and growth ranges, and the economic regime: what each reads and when it is shown.
help.summary_figures-made-for-display: Charts, starting figures, your usual figures and the reference library: numbers shown beside the model's.
help.summary_regional-differences-at-a-glance: What changes with the country, currency or accounting standard, in one table.
help.summary_model-validation: How the model's risk read is checked against what really happened.
help.summary_ml-evaluation-and-model-cards: How every estimate is tested against a simple baseline before it is shown.
help.summary_known-limitations: The model's known shortcuts, open until they are fixed.
help.summary_constants: Every fixed number the calculations use.
help.summary_settings-defaults: The default value of every Setting.

whatsNew.onboardingTitle: Guided first deal, sample deals and help
whatsNew.onboardingBody: Start a deal from four answers, open sample deals from six countries, read how every number is calculated under Help, and hover any input's label for a tip.
whatsNew.explanationsBody: An Explain button on the main tiles says what the figures mean, quoting them exactly, and every label shows its definition on hover.
whatsNew.documentToDealBody: Upload an annual report or information pack in any language and see every value with its page and quote; only the values you accept enter the deal.
whatsNew.resultsNoteBody: Draft a results note from a covered company's saved model as Word or PDF. Every figure comes from the model; the rating, target and argument are yours.
whatsNew.valuationTitle: Valuation and two more sector models
whatsNew.valuationBody: Every sector model now values the company by discounted cash flow and a target multiple, and per-tonne and stores models join the occupancy model.
whatsNew.sectorModelsBody: Build a company's model as live Excel formulas from its accepted results, change its revenue lines, and save it back from Excel.
whatsNew.excelAddinBody: Sign in from Excel, import a company's checked results and load its model straight into a workbook.
whatsNew.documentsBody: Keep the PDFs, workbooks and Word files behind a deal, each checked before it can be opened.
whatsNew.liveSlidersBody: Move growth, the exit multiple, rates, margin or leverage and see the simulated return for your own deal at once.
whatsNew.usualFiguresBody: Beside the sourced figures, the medians of your own saved deals in the same region and sector.
